notes.kabaka: Le Kabaka; the French word for king is le roi.
notes.ssaabasajja: Sa Majesté: feminine, even for a king.
notes.katikkiro: Le Premier ministre, with a capital P.
notes.edda-ennyo: Il y a très longtemps, or in tales, Il était une fois.

guidebook.intro: Meet the Kabaka and the history of Buganda. History books in French use a past tense you’ll only read, not say.

tips.title: Kintu fut le premier Kabaka
body: Written history and tales use the **passé simple**: **Kintu fut le premier Kabaka** (Kintu was the first Kabaka), **Le roi appela Abunuwasi** (the king called Abunuwasi). In speech, people use the passé composé instead: **Le roi a appelé Abunuwasi.**
You only need to recognise it. The **il** forms end in **-a** (for -er verbs), **-it** or **-ut**: **il parla, il partit, il fut**.

tips.title: Titles and kings
body: Titles are lower case in French: **le roi, la reine, le Premier ministre**. **Sa Majesté** (His/Her Majesty) uses **sa** because **majesté** is feminine, even for a king.
**Vive le roi !** (long live the king!) is a fixed old form; for several, **Vivent les mariés !**

tips.title: Abunuwasi était très malin
body: Describing someone in the past uses the imperfect: **Abunuwasi était très malin** (was very clever), **Le royaume était grand.** Events use the passé composé or, in books, the passé simple.

culture.title: Kingdoms in the francophone world
body: Traditional kings still matter in many francophone countries: the **Mogho Naba** of the Mossi in Burkina Faso, the sultans of northern Cameroon, and the **rois** of Benin’s old kingdoms.
